Hacked Off
HAKT OFF
adjective (Boomer slang)
From hack, to cut roughly (Old English haccian; Webster 1828: "to cut irregularly and into small pieces"), with the figurative sense of being cut up, irritated. Hacked off and hacked, meaning annoyed or angry, are mid-twentieth-century American slang, in common Boomer use by the 1960s–70s ("I was really hacked off about it"); compare ticked off and teed off. The British phrase hacked off, fed up, is similar.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To be hacked off is to be annoyed, irritated, angry — not quite furious, but definitely not happy. "Dad was hacked off about the dent in the car." The Christian observation: Scripture speaks to the everyday anger the slang names with more precision than we usually do. It does not say all anger is sin. "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Eph 4:26). There is a righteous anger at evil. But most of what we call being hacked off is not righteous; it is wounded pride, frustrated plans, and impatience. James is plain: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:19–20). God put a question to the angry prophet Jonah that every hacked-off father should hear: "Doest thou well to be angry?" (Jon 4:4). Jonah was hacked off because God was merciful to his enemies and because a plant that shaded him died; God asked him to look at his anger honestly. Proverbs gives the way out: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (Pro 15:1); and "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression" (Pro 19:11). A father who is hacked off about a dented fender and chooses to pass over it, after the facts are known, is showing his son something of the patience of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Mid-20th-c. American slang (from hack, to cut roughly) for annoyed or angry — everyday anger Scripture permits only without sin (Eph 4:26), questions ("Doest thou well to be angry?" Jon 4:4), and answers with the glory of passing over a transgression (Pro 19:11).

HACKED OFF, adj. (American slang, mid-20th c.; common Boomer use 1960s–70s) Annoyed, irritated, angry. Also hacked. Compare ticked off, teed off.

Webster (1828) — HACK, verb transitive 1. To cut irregularly and into small pieces; to notch; to mangle by repeated strokes of a cutting instrument.

Decode for families: name the anger, then ask Jonah’s question.

Modern Corruption

The slang treats everyday anger as a normal mood to be announced; Scripture asks whether the anger is righteous, forbids nursing it, and commends the soft answer and the passing over of offenses.

expand to see more

Our language has dozens of mild words for anger — hacked off, ticked off, ticked, miffed, steamed — and their mildness can hide the seriousness of the thing. A man who is "just a little hacked off" all the time is a man whose household walks on eggshells. Scripture takes the low-grade, chronic irritability of a home seriously, because it poisons love slowly. Eph 4:26 sets a daily deadline: deal with it before sundown.

Jonah’s story is the best mirror. He was angry at God’s mercy and angry about his own comfort, and God answered him not with a lecture but with a question (Jon 4:4) and a lesson in compassion. The gospel answers our anger the same way: we who have been forgiven an enormous debt are asked to pass over the small ones (Pro 19:11).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English haccian (to cut in pieces) → hack (to cut roughly; 1828) → mid-20th-c. American slang hacked (off) (annoyed).
